name: Error Rates Must Drop 100x
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: One Wrong Move in a Thousand: Why Quantum Error Rates Are Still Too High
lesson.summary: Today's best quantum processors get a physical operation wrong roughly once in every few hundred to a thousand tries, and useful, large-scale fault-tolerant computing is widely estimated, in rough ballpark terms, to need those error rates to fall by something like another one to two orders of magnitude.
lesson.body:
The earlier chapter on the error rate problem explained why quantum computing hardware is so much less reliable than classical computing hardware. Classical bits are, for practical purposes, essentially error-free, modern classical computers run trillions of operations without a meaningful chance of a stray error. Physical qubits are nowhere near that reliable, because every operation performed on a qubit, a single-qubit gate, a two-qubit gate, a measurement, carries a real chance of introducing an error, since qubits are extremely sensitive to noise from their surrounding environment, the same fragility that shows up in the decoherence problem discussed later in this unit.

Where does the hardware actually stand today, stated carefully and with real hedging attached? Across the leading platforms, superconducting circuits, trapped ions, and others, two-qubit gate error rates on the best current devices are commonly reported somewhere in the range of a few tenths of a percent up to around one percent, depending heavily on the specific platform and even the specific device generation. Put roughly, that is somewhere around one error in every few hundred to one thousand operations. This number should be read as illustrative rather than as a single fixed figure, since it varies substantially by hardware type and keeps shifting as devices improve.

Why does this matter so much for building a genuinely useful machine? Quantum error correction schemes, the surface code being the most widely discussed example, work by encoding one logical, error-protected qubit across many physical qubits and continuously checking for and correcting errors as the computation runs. But this only works at all if the physical error rate is below what is called a threshold. Above that threshold, adding more physical qubits per logical qubit actually makes things worse, since you are just adding more opportunities for errors without gaining enough correcting power to offset them. Below the threshold, the logical error rate falls off rapidly as you add more physical qubits per logical qubit, meaning the error correction genuinely works and gets better as you scale it up. Being only just barely below threshold is not good enough for a practical machine, though, because it still requires an enormous number of physical qubits to protect each logical qubit well enough to be useful. The further below threshold the physical hardware operates, the fewer physical qubits are needed per logical qubit, which is why the field cares about not just crossing the threshold but getting meaningfully further beneath it.

This is where the roughly one hundred times figure comes from, and it deserves to be stated as exactly what it is: a rough, widely cited estimate from the research community, not a precise engineering specification. Getting from today's typical physical error rates, very roughly one error in a few hundred to one in a thousand operations, down to the range that would let fault-tolerant computing work with a manageable number of physical qubits per logical qubit, very roughly one error in tens of thousands up to one in a million depending on the assumptions used, represents something in the ballpark of one to two orders of magnitude of improvement, commonly summarized in the field as needing error rates to drop by about one hundred times. The precise number depends heavily on which kind of error you are measuring, gate error, readout error, or idle error while a qubit sits unused, which hardware platform you are talking about, which error-correcting code is being used, and how much physical qubit overhead you are willing to accept, so this should be treated as an order-of-magnitude signpost rather than a specific target any single device needs to hit.

Connecting back to the previous chapter on the required breakthroughs, this is one of the three most quantifiable pieces of that broader cluster of problems. Unlike a marketing claim about a rising qubit count, an error rate improvement of this scale requires genuine, hard-won gains in materials science, fabrication precision, and control engineering, the slow, unglamorous kind of progress that does not make for an easy headline. That is exactly the kind of evidence a skeptical reader should look for, peer-reviewed, independently reported error rate measurements, before crediting any announcement that fault-tolerant quantum computing is arriving imminently.
